entries.title: The Real Threat to the Midterms Is Regular Americans Thinking Violence Is the Answer
entries.summary: Robert A. Pape, a leading authority on political violence, wants Americans to understand that the threat is coming not from the fringes, but from the mainstream.
entries.content:
The attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021, was not conducted mainly by extremists or fringe militia groups. It was, according to the data, the work of normal Americans.

That is the conclusion Robert A. Pape lays out in his new book, Our Own Worst Enemies: America in the Age of Violent Populism, citing data about those who were arrested and charged following the attack.

While Proud Boys and Oath Keepers gained most of the headlines, data collected by Pape as part of his work as founding director of the Chicago Project on Security and Threats (CPOST) found that the vast majority (90 percent) of those charged with crimes arising from the attack held no affiliation with militias or militant organizations.

Pape’s analysis found that 22 percent were business owners, and almost 30 percent held a college degree. Among the defendants were doctors, engineers, CEOs, and government employees. Nearly 40 percent held white-collar jobs, while just 8 percent of participants were unemployed.

The findings are key to understanding the warning that is central to Pape’s book: Americans do not understand that the threat of political violence is coming not from the fringes, but from the mainstream.

“As the 2026 midterms approach, US elections are entering a danger zone in which state power, protest, and political legitimacy increasingly collide,” Pape writes in the book. “For most Americans, political violence is still understood as episodic—shocking when it erupts but destined to fade. That assumption is reassuring. It is also increasingly dangerous.”

WIRED spoke to Pape about his book, his concerns about violence in the midterms, why it is so important to understand the attack on the Capitol, and what, if anything, gives him hope that democracy will win out.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

DAVID GILBERT: Your book is centered on the idea of violent populism. What is it, and why is it on the rise in 2026?

ROBERT A. PAPE: Violent populism is a dangerous political climate where substantial segments of the public increasingly accept physical force as a legitimate tool to gain, preserve, or defend political power. It is on the rise due to a profound cultural clash over the nature of American identity and citizenship, exacerbated by elite rhetoric that frames politics as an existential struggle between enemies. This structural dynamic transforms ordinary, mainstream citizens into active participants in political aggression.

You call the midterms “a stress test of whether American competition can remain bounded by nonviolence.” Are you concerned about the political violence around this election?

Yes, the level of concern for this election cycle is at an unprecedented high, surpassing anything seen since the deep social upheavals of the 1960s. With national anxieties amplified by a highly combustible domestic climate and global instability like the ongoing war with Iran, elections have increasingly become dangerous potential flashpoints. This dynamic represents a direct, critical test of whether our foundational institutions can still successfully enforce peaceful political transitions.

Heading into the midterms, a lot of people are focusing on possible action from extremist groups, such as militias. Is this the wrong thing to be worried about?

Focusing exclusively on fringe militias misdiagnoses the primary danger facing American democracy today. The real threat is that political radicalization has broken out of the fringes and fully migrated into the mainstream electorate. Our primary worry should be the tens of millions of ordinary Americans who now passively accept or actively endorse violence to achieve their political goals.

You write that Americans are misreading the warning signs of political violence, again. What are those warning signs?

The primary warning sign is the broad public normalization and passive acceptance of aggressive political acts as standard features of daily political life. This is signaled by an explosion of violent symbolism across the entire media spectrum and elite rhetoric that strips legitimacy away from opposing factions. When ordinary citizens begin to view political opposition as an existential, hostile force, the ground is fully prepared for real-world conflict.

You write in the book that the January 6th attack on the Capitol was a rubicon crossed between "routine political conflict and civil war." Why was it such an important turning point?

The January 6th attack shattered the all-important democratic norm that power changes hands through ballots rather than raw displays of physical coercion. It demonstrated that an electoral outcome could be violently challenged not by foreign adversaries, but by a massive crowd of American citizens targeting their own legislative body. This crossed line signaled that internal political disputes were no longer reliably bounded by a shared commitment to nonviolence.

The narrative around the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol is that it was driven by extremist groups on the fringes of American society. But that's not what the data shows, right?

CPOST data completely disproves the fringe narrative by showing the remarkable mainstream geography of those involved in the insurrection. The vast majority of the actors were not isolated radicals or card-carrying militia members, but “normal” political activists with stable homes, jobs, and 401(k)s. Only 1 in 10 were militia members. Nearly half were doctors, lawyers, CEOs, business owners, US State Department appointees—and some even attended the White House Christmas party the year before. Most represented a cross-section of middle-class America acting on a shared, mainstream belief that democratic institutions were no longer legitimate.

Why do you think the prevailing narrative around the January 6 attack on the Capitol has been so wrong for so many years?

The narrative has been wrong because public institutions and media outlets initially relied heavily on imperfect law enforcement databases that naturally isolated the most prominent, organized fringe actors. And they did not update their readers and viewers as the bulk of the data came in. This approach ignored the underlying, broader structural dynamics of public opinion and extensive survey research. By focusing strictly on the visible, oddball characters, analysts missed the massive wave of passive, mainstream support that actually fueled the event.

My reading of this book is that most people have a fundamental misunderstanding of political violence in America in 2026. Is that accurate?

That is completely accurate and is the central, urgent argument of the entire book. The greatest threat to the United States is not an out-of-control group of radical extremists, but the reality that millions of otherwise ordinary citizens now accept violence as a regular political tool. Once political violence is normalized by the mainstream, old institutional solutions cease to function effectively.

You compare the current embrace of violent populism by middle-class white America to the expansion of the second Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s. Do you think people will be shocked by that comparison?

Many readers will likely be shocked, because the modern imagination associates the Klan strictly with regional, low-income hate groups rather than a massive social movement. However, the historical data shows that the second KKK of the 1920s was a highly mainstream, middle-class organization driven by a cultural clash over American identity. Drawing this explicit parallel highlights how easily normal, institutionalized communities can slide into systemic intolerance when they feel their cultural dominance is threatened.

Do you think readers of the book will be surprised that defense of political violence is not solely the preserve of the right, but that people on the left also reinforce your thesis of violent populism?

Yes, readers who expect a one-sided partisan critique will be surprised to see that the call for political violence comes from both sides of the aisle. [Confessed health care CEO assassin Luigi] Mangione and the recent [accused] Trump assassin at the April White House Correspondents’ Dinner reflect political violence from the left, and they are far from alone. Original CPOST surveys reveal that violent style, aggressive symbolism, and the demonization of political opponents are heavily utilized by figures across the entire political spectrum. This multisided reality proves that violent populism is a systemic, societal failure rather than an isolated partisan phenomenon.

You say that it is not yet determined if the current transitional phase of American politics will “culminate in democratic renewal or deeper political breakdown.” Do you have a sense of when we might have an answer to this question?

We need to lean into the “good news” in my book: that 70 percent of Americans abhor political violence. This is the large, untapped resource that we need to lean into. My book is essentially for the 70 percent and a call to action for what they can do—beyond voting. The 70 percent are the heart of our democracy. Leaning into them is how we save our democracy and avoid a much deeper, systemic breakdown of American governance.

What, if anything, gives you hope that violent populism can be overcome?

Hope lies in the data that can give new active optimism to vast majorities of ordinary Americans on both the left and right that still share a fundamental desire for stability and governance. By recognizing that our enemies are not really each other, but the normalization of violence itself, we can deliberately choose strategies of restraint to rebuild our vital democratic norms—and find productive new solutions.

entries.title: Tractive Cat 6 Mini Review: A Fitbit for Your Cat
entries.summary: Cats are finally getting the dog treatment. This smart cat collar features GPS location, activity, and sleep tracking, plus all-new heart and respiratory rate monitoring.
entries.content:
As the pet tech industry expands rapidly, pet owners are more eager to adopt technology that tracks health metrics, similar to human wearable devices like smart rings, smartwatches, and fitness trackers.

I've been testing smart collars for the better part of the year, previously testing the Fi Mini and Tractive Smart Cat Tracker on my cat Basil, which monitored his location, movement, and sleep.

The Tractive Cat 6 Mini was released this spring, and I tested it on Basil for a month, comparing how this new-and-improved smart collar made specifically for cats with improved health features, like heart and respiratory rate, stacked up against other models.

This new model had surprisingly accurate health and activity stats that helped me understand Basil's routine and baseline a bit more than the previous models I've tested. I think these new health features would be especially helpful for people with aging cats or cats in poor health. (If you have an outdoor cat that roams, I'd go with the Fi Mini because it's more compact with a longer battery life.)

I valued the Cat 6 Mini's new AI-powered weekly reports and comparisons to similar cats to know if Basil is healthy. However, the collar itself died quickly, was a pain to charge, and GPS location accuracy could be hit-or-miss. Whether this smart cat collar is the right fit for you largely depends on your and your cat's needs.

entries.title: Exclusive: Neurable’s First Brain-Scanning Headphones Want to Fine-Tune Your Focus
entries.summary: The company claims that its new device, the Neurable One, can keep you in the zone, calculate the best time to take a break, and tell you when your “brain battery” needs a recharge.
entries.content:
Neurable unveiled its very own pair of brain-scanning headphones on Thursday, the Neurable One. The company claims that wearing them helps you concentrate on whatever you’re doing—working, studying, or playing a video game.

When I spoke to Neurable earlier this year, the company said it planned to license its brain-scanning technology to power a flood of gadgets that were ready to enter the market. But it decided to launch its own hardware first.

“We wanted to take the product in-house,” Ramses Alcaide, Neurable’s cofounder and CEO, tells WIRED. “There were a lot of areas where we wanted to improve the product, and we wanted to move at a much faster rate. It also puts a little more capability for us to be able to show off what’s possible with the technology.”

The Boston company has until now relied on other brands to showcase its brain-scanning technology in their products, all of which promise to help people improve focus and provide data about your brain activity in a companion app. It began a few years ago by building its tech into some Master & Dynamic headphones. At the start of this year, Neurable showed off a gaming headset with HP's HyperX featuring two electroencephalography (EEG) sensors built in.

Like the original M&D MW75 Neuro headphones, the Neurable One features 12 EEG sensors in the nylon earpads that are used to monitor brain waves. The headphones cost $499 and will be available in October from Neurable’s website.

Alongside the new headphones is a new app (the old app will continue to exist for now for older hardware), which Alcaide says tracks eight brain metrics:

  • Brain Age: Tracks your brain’s perceived age against your real age.
  • Brain Battery: What you have left in reserve.
  • Speed: How quickly you process information.
  • Focus: How well your attention is holding.
  • Load: How much effort you spend doing the task.
  • Stress: How much tension you have doing the task.
  • Sleepiness: How far you are drifting toward sleep.
  • Alpha Peak Frequency: Your strongest resting rhythm, which Neurable claims is like the brain's heart rate variability.

The biggest hardware and software change with the Neurable One is that you no longer have to start a session in the app to capture brain activity. Instead, the Neurable One passively monitors your brain as soon as you put the headphones on—Alcaide likens it to wearing a Fitbit.

At that point, the sensors begin monitoring your brain activity to measure your focus. When it detects that you’re getting distracted, the headphones play a ping to get you back on track. If it thinks you're burning out instead, it’ll recommend a break so you can come back later fully recharged.

The headphone-app combo works similarly to help you fall asleep and to meditate. For example, with meditation, you can follow a guided session, and when the headphones detect you’re in the flow, the guide will stop talking so you stay in that zone. If it detects you’re drifting away, it’ll start guiding you back again. For sleep—designed for naps rather than proper bedtime—it can, over time, lower the headset volume of guided naps or soundscapes as it detects you falling asleep. (You can also turn off the EEG sensors and just use them as regular headphones if you want.)

Alcaide says when the app tells him his brain battery is low for the day, he’ll go to the sauna and go to bed early to help him recover. It can tell him when his peak brain speed hours are, allowing him to rejigger his schedule so he does his hardest work during those times. There’s also a check-in system called Cognitive Snapshot; when you trigger it, the app shows your current brain state and offers recommendations to improve it. That could be a guided meditation or small games to exercise those parts of your brain. The app also provides weekly or monthly reports to track your brain activity over time.

Neurable doesn’t have any new research or data to share that can speak to the effectiveness of its latest headphones. That research is in the works, but it will take time. So Neurable still points to previous research with the Mayo Clinic, which showed a 30 percent increase in focus in individuals using Neurable's headset versus people using Pomodoro techniques or other types of focus-sustaining systems. The study also saw a drop of about 10 percent in end-of-day burnout and an increase in end-of-day happiness.

The product isn’t categorized as a medical device, and Neurable says it isn’t designed to diagnose, treat, or monitor any conditions. The company also promises not to sell any of the data it collects about your brain—which could become very valuable in the future—and says it doesn't use that data for advertising. Alcaide says enterprise customers buy its headsets in bulk to help employees focus, but they’re not buying the headsets to monitor the workforce.

“It's because we know we're going to get higher productivity per employee; they're going to be happier, they're going to feel less burned out, it's a win-win for everybody,” he says. “It's like how sometimes companies get gym memberships for their employees.” He stresses that each user’s data stays with them.

Alcaide says the company partnered with an audio brand to help with the non-brain-scanning bits of the hardware, though he wouldn’t share the name. These cans have the “same premium sound” as the earlier M&D collaboration, with 40-mm beryllium drivers, six microphones, active noise cancellation, a transparency mode, and 22 hours of run time—12 if you have those EEG sensors running. It supports Bluetooth 5.2, and both AAC and aptX codecs. Neurable’s app is available on both Android and iOS.

entries.title: Madison Square Garden’s James Dolan Is Spending Big on New York’s Governor Race
entries.summary: James Dolan has put surveillance at the center of his sports and entertainment empire. Now he’s getting involved in GOP politics by backing a candidate who supports Flock, ICE, and AI data centers.
entries.content:
Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for New York governor, promised last November to erect a wall of spy gear, license plate readers, and biometric surveillance between the city and the suburbs. He has since received millions of dollars in donations from the family and businesses of James Dolan, the owner of Madison Square Garden, where a network of cameras capture the faces of (nearly) every patron who walks in the arena and corporate security forces hunt for critics of the boss.

Dolan’s support of Blakeman, the executive of suburban Nassau County, could be seen as something of a counterintuitive move in a state long run by Democrats, and in a year when political surveys are picking up indications of a blue wave. He’s down by nine points or more in most polls.

Blakeman, however, backs data centers, AI deepfakes, Flock surveillance, ICE, private militias, and president Donald Trump. All of which makes him at least somewhat simpatico with Dolan, the Trump-allied magnate operating the sports world’s best-known surveillance state. Dolan has long been a mercurial presence in the political game, and in fact, as Politico notes, he supported Blakeman’s opponent, Governor Kathy Hochul, during the last election. Dolan’s sheer amount of spending in the race could also benefit him, even if his preferred candidate loses.

Long an outsized force in sports and entertainment, Dolan now has a chance at a major political role, too.

“Dolan can step into the breach and become the biggest player in [New York’s] Republican politics, donor-wise, and I'm sure his people are smart enough to know that,” one veteran strategist tells WIRED.

James Dolan has given heavily before, including nearly a million dollars to Trump’s reelection campaign and the Republican National Committee in the 2020 election cycle. But the New York governor’s race represents another level, a review of city, state, and federal databases shows.

The Dolan family has given $108,000 to Blakeman’s campaign directly and another $970,000 to the local Nassau County Republican party, which in turn has become Blakeman’s single-largest contributor. But that’s just for starters. MSG entities have contributed another $2 million to a political action committee supporting Blakeman’s run. That super PAC, Strong and Safe New York Inc., which lists Madison Square Garden’s top government relations executive as an officer, has raised $5.3 million overall. That helped make up for a 9-to-1 cash advantage that the governor’s campaign reported over her challenger’s at the last filing deadline in July.

Dolan and MSG’s bankrolling of Blakeman could come with risks, however. Opposition to Dolan’s use of facial recognition has hit a new peak locally, where a majority of the City Council are now in favor of a bill to rein in biometric surveillance. State lawmakers introduced a bill to end the property tax break that has been worth over a billion dollars to Madison Square Garden. The federal government has agreed to take over the $8 billion renovation of the train station below Madison Square Garden—a project that could pay Dolan’s company $500 million or more. But multiple sources note that state and local authorities will likely continue to have a say.

Meanwhile, the New York attorney general’s investigation into MSG’s deployment of facial recognition continues to progress, a source familiar with the matter tells WIRED. And while mayor Zohran Mamdani’s critiques of Dolan’s security practices have been muted, so far, there are signs that may be changing. One of his commissioners said last month that “this kind of mass surveillance opens the door to abuse and discrimination.”

(Madison Square Garden, which did not respond to a request to comment for this story, filed a defamation suit in July against WIRED and this reporter over our coverage of its operations.)

Dolan’s friction with state and local officials is coming at what should be a peak moment for the mogul: the long-suffering basketball team he owns, the New York Knicks, recently won their first title in 53 years. And yet, during the Knicks’ run in the NBA Finals, his organization fought with the mayor and the police commissioner over security procedures around the Garden. In the days leading up to the championship parade down Broadway, a source with knowledge of the preparations tells WIRED, Dolan’s team tussled with the governor’s and the mayor’s for control over the event, particularly over who got to be on stage and in the audience as the players were presented with keys to the city at City Hall.

“Dolan micromanaged the Knicks parade like it was his own sweet sixteen,” the source tells WIRED.

Dolan and Blakeman, on the other hand, have in recent years demonstrated a host of common interests, common enemies, and one extremely prominent mutual friend. In June, Trump came to the Garden for game three of the Finals; Blakeman joined the president of the United States and the team’s owner in the luxury box. Two months later, in mid-August, Strong and Safe New York released an ad calling on Hochul to stop blaming the state’s problems on Trump. (Strong and Safe, which is also supporting James’ opponent in the attorney general’s race this year, recently sent $83,400 to her former employers, the Republican law firm behind Kanye West’s presidential bid in 2020.)

Blakeman has been one of the state’s most enthusiastic implementers of Trump’s mass deportation machine, ordering local detectives to work with ICE and opening up the county’s jails for those caught up in the crackdown. (Less than 5 percent of the immigrants jailed had violent criminal records, a Newsday investigation found.) He recruited dozens of armed “special deputies,” which looked a whole lot like a personal militia to critics. And when Mamdani won his New York mayoral election last November, Blakeman promised to erect a wall of surveillance along the city line to keep suburban residents safe. “We are installing technology along the border of New York City that will read license plates, that will have facial recognition, that will have video cameras,” he told Fox News. Since then, drivers in Nassau County have become some of the most surveilled in the nation, with a Flock Safety camera for every 9.5 miles of road, according to the DeFlock activist group.

Dolan has been aggressive in his deployment of surveillance at his venues, which include the Sphere in Las Vegas and Radio City Music Hall in Manhattan. Arrays of surveillance security cameras tied to a video management system running a facial recognition program are a major reason why MSG “is the most secure venue in the country,” Dolan has previously said.

“They’re in the same mindset that surveillance is good for business,” Brad Hoylman-Sigal, the Manhattan borough president, says of Blakeman and Dolan. “And I don’t know how that's a winning political issue.”

For the majority of more than three decades in politics, Blakeman presented himself as a moderate as he launched unsuccessful bids for state comptroller, US House and Senate seats, and even New York City mayor. Then in 2021, Blakeman went full MAGA, and won his Nassau County Executive race by 2,000 votes. He’s been tied to Trump and the Trumpists ever since, starting with an all-out push behind MAGA megadonor Miriam Adelson’s multibillion plan to build a casino on the site of the Nassau Coliseum. The bid was ultimately withdrawn.

Hochul’s recent political journey has gone in something like the opposite direction. Once considered a conservative Democrat, she’s become a vocal Trump critic; passed a law banning local cops from cooperating with ICE (a move Blakeman said was “written with the blood of the victims of illegal migrants,” before reluctantly complying with it; and put in place the country’s first statewide data center moratorium (Blakeman called that “crazy,” while using AI to lampoon Hochul in his TV spots).

Dolan largely stayed out of last year’s mayor’s race. But an MSG political action committee, the Coalition to Restore New York, dumped more than $400,000 into 11 local City Council races. Seven of them won, and all but one lined up to support Julie Menin as City Council president, who was seen as a check on Mamdani’s power.

Menin now holds the power to bring the Council’s bill curbing facial recognition to a vote—or to let it die without one. Menin, who returned a Dolan donation in 2023, is currently undecided on how to proceed, the veteran strategist tells me. “She doesn't want to ban facial recognition”—and to be clear, the bill in the Council doesn’t aim to do that. “She thinks that it should be reformed, and that there should be guardrails and parameters,” the strategist says. (A Menin spokesperson did not reply to a request for comment.)

One longtime outside counsel for MSG has filed a flurry of lawsuits against the Mamdani administration, while a second former outside attorney has raised a million dollars for a political organization to counter the mayor’s agenda. John Catsimatidis, a billionaire Republican donor, indicated to Politico that Dolan’s backing of Blakeman could be seen as a move against Mamdani, of sorts. “Everybody believes the governor has oversight of the mayor,” he said. (Representatives for both the Hochul and Blakeman campaigns did not respond to requests to comment for this story. Neither did a City Hall spokesperson. But Mamdani did say on Monday that a candidate "who embraces ICE and has gone so far as to create, effectively, a private militia in Nassau County” is “in many ways the antithesis” of what New Yorkers want.)

The governor is not without her own well-funded allies, however. That includes Blakeman’s ex-wife Nancy Shevell, who’s now married to Paul McCartney. She donated $18,000 to Hochul. The Pegula family, which owns the NFL’s Buffalo Bills, has given her and the state Democratic Party nearly $175,000. (A small sum to pay, considering Hochul helped steer $600 million in state money into her hometown team’s new stadium.) Uber spent more than $12 million in a six-month period to a PAC supporting Hochul, who has proposed auto insurance reforms that the ride-share giant likes.

That’s way more than Dolan has devoted to his candidate so far. But what he has given appears to be the most money a Dolan-backed business has devoted to a political cause since it spent an estimated $30 million in 2004 to stop a football stadium from being built on Manhattan’s west side, a signature project by the mayor at the time, Michael Bloomberg. Dolan’s push was so effective, it caused the mayor to sputter in public. “You’d think,” the mayor fumed on his radio program, that “a company on corporate welfare would be less selfish to the city that has been so good to it.”

For that campaign, Dolan’s firm funded an outfit called the “New York Association for Better Choices,” which took out full-page ads in every city newspaper, ran anti-stadium commercials on local TV, and counted the lobbying firm of a former US senator as one of its many advocates. For this election, Dolan’s chosen candidate is relying heavily on AI. Blakeman’s ads featuring ersatz Hochuls hiding behind dumpsters, getting clowned by Mamdani, and producing BS. One recent anti-Hochul spot lifted footage from a comedian’s bit—shot in 2011 and criticizing the Republican leader of Wisconsin at the time. “Bruce Blakeman,” the progressive local news outlet Hell Gate proclaimed, “is the governor of slop.”

entries.title: Apple Mac Studio (M5 Ultra) Review: Unlimited Power
entries.summary: The Mac Studio can run frontier-level AI language models locally. It’s only a preview of what’s to come.
entries.content:
Over in Draw Things, I ran some on-device image and video generation to really see what an 80-core GPU can do. Using the MiniMax H3 model, it took over 11 minutes to generate a 15-second video completely on-device. There's a long way to go before this feels like a viable alternative to cloud-based options or needing a high-powered discrete GPU like an RTX 5090 or 5080 for this kind of task. Obviously, paying this much to run AI locally is a niche endeavor. But as models get more efficient and quality improves, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio's capabilities should improve over time. We're still in the early days.

During these AI tests, in particular, I noticed how warm the Mac Studio gets when it's fully under load. You definitely don't want to touch it or set anything on top of it. You also want to leave some room behind it, since it blows a lot of hot air out of the vents. The fans can spin up quite loudly too—though, like all modern Macs, it takes a couple of minutes for the fans to really get going. The front-facing ports stay cool, though, thanks to the vents in the thermal system sitting right underneath the Mac Studio.

Only the Beginning

The Mac Studio is certainly unique. Because mini Windows PCs typically use laptop chips, they don't typically support more than 64 GB of RAM. That's where this top-end M5 Ultra Mac Studio really feels unbeatable (and even earns its sky-high price from that perspective). Add the upcoming option for 512 GB of memory (and the ability to connect four Mac Studios and use them as a single computer), and you have something extremely niche—but wholly unrivaled.

The base M5 Max Mac Studio does have stronger competition, though. For $2,399, you can get a Geekom A9 Mega Mini PC with 64 GB of RAM, 1 TB of storage, and AMD's new Ryzen AI Max+ 388. That's more memory and more storage for less money. Importantly, that AMD chip uses unified memory the same way Apple Silicon does, which is crucial for running local AI workloads. We'll hopefully be getting the Geekom A9 in for testing to see how it stacks up in real-world tests.

More competitors are coming soon, too. Nvidia's RTX Spark “superchips” are the main upcoming rival, offering up to 128 GB of unified memory in both laptops and mini PCs. They still can't do 256 GB of memory like the Mac Studio, but these will hopefully turn up the heat on the Windows and Linux side.

entries.title: The Secrets of the US Spyware King
entries.summary: In an exclusive interview with WIRED, Paragon Solutions CEO Andrew Boyd reveals the limits of the company’s promise to keep bad actors from abusing its powerful espionage tool.
entries.content:
Spyware maker Paragon Solutions has long positioned itself as the good guy in an industry seemingly filled with bad ones, vowing to never sell its mobile spyware to authoritarian regimes or ones with poor human rights records. It also promises to cut off any customer caught misusing its products against journalists, dissidents, or other non-legitimate targets.

Yet weeks after Paragon, then Israeli-owned, was acquired by the US equity firm AE Industrial Partners in December 2024 and merged with REDLattice—an American offensive cyber firm owned by AE that this week announced plans to go public—WhatsApp alleged that Paragon’s Graphite spyware was used to infect the phones of more than 60 individuals in more than 20 countries, including journalists and activists. Most of the targets were not identified, but the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab named two journalists and two activists in Italy.

Italian authorities denied misuse. Paragon and its new US owners, despite their zero-tolerance policy for customer abuse of their software, initially declined to comment on the allegations, and reportedly was exploring potential legal action against WhatsApp after the company sent a cease-and-desist letter to Paragon. Within a week, however, Paragon had canceled the two contracts it had with Italy’s domestic and foreign intelligence agencies.

From the outside, it seemed Paragon must have conducted an investigation and verified the allegations before canceling the contracts. But Paragon and RedLattice’s new CEO, Andrew Boyd, now says in an exclusive and surprisingly candid interview with WIRED that the company simply “fired” Italy because it “just was not worth it, from a risk perspective, to maintain the relationship” following the allegations.

In other words, there was no Paragon investigation and no interest in conducting one to determine if the allegations were true—Italian government investigators concluded they were not. Paragon didn’t even follow up with WhatsApp or Citizen Lab to obtain details about the alleged abuse and determine if any contracts in the other countries named by WhatsApp should be canceled as well. More damning, according to critics, is what Boyd revealed next: Paragon has no technical way to know if customers misuse its software, because it can’t see who customers target or the data they extract from targeted devices. It can only learn about misuse if customers admit to it or third parties uncover it. He says WhatsApp and Citizen Lab did the company a great service when they exposed the alleged misuse last year.

Paragon also doesn’t have a “kill switch” to disable customers when misuse occurs. All they can do is halt customers’ 24-hour support and system “updates.” But Boyd says the updates, the nature of which he won’t specify, are frequent and essential to using the spyware, and without them the system is rendered ineffective in about 12 hours.

“Things start falling apart quite quickly,” he says.

Boyd’s comments mark the first time a Paragon executive has spoken in detail about the secretive company or its handling of the Italian affair. He agreed to speak with WIRED now because he says more public discussion is needed about the offensive cyber industry and what it means for a US company to operate responsibly in this space. Prior to the interview, REDLattice founder John Ayers wrote in an email that they were “not looking for a favorable write-up.”

“If the honest assessment is still damning, that's a conversation we're prepared to have,” he wrote.

But Boyd’s admissions reveal that despite priding itself on being better than competitors, Paragon/RedLattice has less oversight and accountability than its most significant one—NSO Group, the Pegasus spyware maker, which has been excoriated for selling its tool to Saudi Arabia and other countries with poor human rights records. According to NSO’s transparency reports, which the company began publishing in recent years in response to criticism, it sets up infrastructure and portals that customers use to infect targets and, like Paragon, can’t see who customers target or detect misuse. But it claims it does have a kill switch to disable a customer’s access to the spyware if allegations of misuse arise, and NSO says its systems keep “tamper-proof” logs to record user activity. Customers are contractually obligated to provide these to NSO if allegations of misuse occur or else face “immediate suspension.”​​

By contrast, Boyd says Paragon customers can enable logging on some systems if they opt to, but Paragon has no access to the logs, nor does it want access. Instead, he says, government oversight bodies can use the logs to investigate allegations of misuse among their agencies, as an Italian parliamentary committee did last year in the case of the Citizen Lab allegations. However, this raises the possibility that a government investigator could lie about misuse if they uncover it in logs.

Rather than see Paragon’s lack of access to logs as an accountability problem, however, Boyd describes it as a selling point: No one would buy their products if the company could see a customer’s sensitive targeting information or logs that contain it.

“There's a balancing act between privacy and security and being able to ensure that our customers are using these things correctly,” Boyd says. “And I think we've landed on the best balance.”

That balance is achieved mostly through careful vetting of customers, he says, and rejecting any country that might be prone to abusing the spyware.

John Scott-Railton, senior researcher at Citizen Lab, which has tracked government misuse of commercial spyware for years, calls the revelations astonishing and the lack of mandatory logging “reckless.”

“What Paragon is saying in several substantial ways means [it has] less oversight, less transparency, less contractual protection against abuses than NSO Group,” he says. “It’s exactly the opposite of the picture that Paragon has painted for itself for years. The CEO admitting that his customers won’t tolerate oversight is refreshing honesty: Accountability is bad for business. And it signals to lawmakers and regulators that the spyware industry cannot be trusted to self-regulate."

Scott-Railton also finds it ironic that Paragon relies on Citizen Lab and others to uncover customer misuse when Paragon actively works to hide its spyware on infected devices and prevent discovery—which inherently includes potential misuse.

“We only find a very, very, very small subset [of infections], and the total numbers are always larger,” Scott-Railton says. “These companies spend millions trying to hide from us.”

US senator Ron Wyden tells WIRED that surveillance tools that lack oversight and transparency are “inevitably abused.”

“It’s easy to claim your powerful hacking tool isn’t being misused if you go out of your way to ensure you don’t know how customers use it,” Wyden says. “The fact that Paragon refuses to audit use of its tool, or even attempt to match the work of a small team of researchers at the Citizen Lab is a massive red flag.”

Israeli Intelligence Roots

Paragon was launched in 2019 by Israeli Brigadier General Ehud Schneorson, former commander of the Israeli military’s signals intelligence group, Unit 8200. He cofounded it with three other 8200 veterans and former Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak. Two years later, the company reportedly had no customers but was developing Graphite and hoping to conquer the lucrative US market. But then the US government began cracking down on foreign spyware companies after NSO’s Pegasus and Candiru’s DevilsTongue tools were misused by their customers against government workers, journalists, dissidents, activists, and academics.

The US Commerce Department sanctioned both companies in 2021, and the Israeli government drastically cut the number of countries to which Israeli firms could sell spyware—from 102 countries to 37, excluding Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Morocco and Mexico. Over a year later, the Biden administration and Congress imposed guardrails making it difficult for the US government to purchase foreign-made commercial spyware if it posed a national security risk or could be misused by foreign governments.

By then, Paragon reportedly already had a contract with the Drug Enforcement Agency to combat drug traffickers outside the US, but otherwise could not “make any substantial headway” in the US, Boyd says. So the company began looking for a US buyer to overcome its foreign-ownership handicap. In December 2024, AE acquired it for $900 million. The result is a company that is now American on paper, but is still effectively Israeli. Paragon is a RedLattice company—though Paragon has no working website, and the RedLattice website currently doesn’t mention Paragon—but, according to Boyd, it retains its name and offices in Israel, where it has more than 600 employees. Any Paragon-built products still require licensing approval from the Israeli government to sell abroad, while RedLattice-made products sold to non-US customers are governed by US International Traffic in Arms Regulations.

Nonetheless, the US acquisition has served as an end-run around foreign-ownership guardrails. Once the AE deal closed, Boyd says, “everybody started talking” to them about Paragon products, and Paragon began looking to hire 150 new workers to handle its expected new business.

Ayers, the REDLattice founder, told WIRED in an email that prior to acquisition, REDLattice and AE spent more than two years in discussion with US and allied governments and “didn't move without their buy-in.” But asked whether the government pushed back on the acquisition, Boyd says there were no objections, and no one imposed conditions or governance requirements on them either.

“The US government in any form [was] never going to formally say … we approve this acquisition,” he says. “But they didn't have any discomfort with it. … If the [National Security Council] said, ‘this would be a colossally bad idea,’ we probably wouldn't have gone through with it.”

Less than a year after Paragon merged with REDLattice, NSO Group and Candiru copied their savvy acquisition move. A US investment group acquired controlling ownership of NSO and appointed David Friedman, former US ambassador to Israel under President Donald Trump, as executive chairman. Candiru was acquired by the US-based Integrity Partners. Now all three companies are vying for US contracts.

Boyd, who became CEO of RedLattice and Paragon eight months after the acquisition, gives the companies an edge in the US market. As a former military intelligence officer, State Department diplomat, and director of the CIA’s Center for Cyber Intelligence until retiring in 2023, he has many US government, military, and intelligence community connections to help secure contracts.

During the interview, Boyd was open with many of WIRED’s questions, but also inexplicably opaque with others. He wouldn’t even, for example, confirm that Graphite is the name of a product the company sells or say how many products the combined companies possess. He says only that before the acquisition, Paragon had fewer than five products and together they now have between five and 10. Some of these do “over-the-horizon” data collection (by hacking devices and systems remotely) while others require physical access to targeted devices. He bristles at calling the tools “spyware,” though. He considers them “defensive” tools since, broadly speaking, they help defend against national security and criminal threats. But in truth, they are designed for surveillance, espionage, and possibly even disruptive cyber operations.

Graphite, the only product ever publicly identified, extracts communications from chat applications, particularly encrypted messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Signal. This contrasts with NSO Group’s Pegasus, which can spy on all aspects of a mobile phone, including surreptitiously activating its microphone and camera to spy on targets. Reportedly, Graphite’s capabilities can be expanded through modules, though its full feature set is not publicly known.

WhatsApp and Citizen Lab have reported that Graphite uses a powerful zero-click zero-day exploit to infect phones without user awareness. Boyd won’t say if the companies hunt for zero-day vulnerabilities and develop their own exploits or purchase them from others, but says both Paragon and RedLattice have “substantial” research and development teams. RedLattice’s website says the company has more than 200 “vulnerability research experts.”

In addition to their products, Paragon and RedLattice build bespoke solutions for some customers, and some contracts provide customers with personnel who possess “appropriate clearances” to do a “variety” of tasks. Boyd won’t elaborate on the tasks but says his company doesn’t do offensive operations for customers; it just provides hardware and software. But after the Trump administration recently announced plans to contract with select private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against cybercriminal groups, he says RedLattice will pursue these contracts.

Customer Vetting

Without the ability to monitor customer activity and detect misuse, Paragon relies on its governance model to prevent abuse. This involves customer vetting and contractual deterrence. Customers, and the countries in which they reside, are vetted by an internal risk committee that Boyd and other board members chair using various criteria to determine if a prospective country or customer might have a negative business or reputational impact on the company.

“We don't want our products to be involved in things that they weren't intended to be used for,” he says.

Boyd wouldn’t provide a full list of the country assessment criteria but mentioned several during the interview: political and government stability, human rights record, corruption-index ratings, strength of a country’s legal system, and whether a potential customer has a track record of adhering to its national laws. He says they lean more toward rejecting countries than approving them. They currently have between 20 and 30 countries on their approved list, and have more than 100 customers in 23 countries.

“I think there's some people that would argue that we're too conservative [about who we’ll sell to],” he says, but notes that “it's better to take a hit on revenue” than sell to countries that could prove detrimental in the long run. (Boyd says, for example, that canceling Italy’s two contracts cost the company “seven figures” in revenue. He would not specify the exact value, but Israeli media have estimated the contracts were worth “tens of millions of dollars.”) In the year since he became CEO, he says a “handful” of countries have been rejected as potential customers but won’t say which ones.

Paragon only sells to the US and select US allies (whether democratic or not) and only to national entities, not state and local governments and police forces. But being a US ally doesn’t guarantee a sale. They won’t sell to Saudi Arabia, even though it’s an ally. After the Saudi government reportedly used NSO’s Pegasus to spy on the fiancé and close associates of Washington Post opinion writer Jamal Khashoggi, who was murdered by Saudi government agents, the Israeli government reportedly asked Paragon to take over the Saudi Arabia contract from NSO Group, but Paragon reportedly refused. Boyd says they still won’t sell to Saudi Arabia, and also says the company has no commercial relationships with any country in the Middle East.

“I think there's very important national security reasons why [the US] would want a close relationship with the Saudis from a nation-state to nation-state level,” he says. But that “does not translate into … this private-sector company having a business relationship with them. … I don't need to get into the why’s, because you probably know the why’s.”

They also won’t sell to Venezuela, even with President Nicolas Maduro gone. “There's too much chaos,” Boyd says, “and it wouldn't fit our risk calculus for other variables.”

Yet the company reportedly signed a lucrative contract in Singapore in 2023 worth tens of millions of dollars. Though an electoral democracy, Singapore imposes significant restrictions on free speech, media independence, and human rights.

The customer vetting, Boyd says, “usually works 99 out of 100 times” to eliminate those who might misuse their tools – the assumption being that if they choose only reputable customers, the customers they choose will act only reputably. For the remaining 1 in 100, the customer contracts and zero-tolerance policy are meant to deter misuse. These prohibit using the tools against journalists, civil society members, opposition politicians, and anyone else who is not the target of a legitimate intelligence or criminal investigation. Also embedded in any system sold to non-US customers is a block that prevents targeting of any person in the US—that is, any number that requires the US +1 country code to dial. US law enforcement agencies who have a warrant can get the block disabled, he says.

What if a US customer let a non-approved country use Graphite to spy on targets? During the first Trump administration, the CIA reportedly purchased NSO Group's Pegasus to give to an East African country to use. Boyd insists they would know if this occurred.

“We know where the system is, because we [help customers] install it and train [them on it]…. And so we would know if it was not installed in the place where they intended it to be,” he insists.

Would they also know if a customer used the tool on their own infrastructure but to spy on behalf of another non-approved country? He says they would, because the majority of customers have similar intelligence, military, or law enforcement backgrounds to RedLattice and Paragon employees, and they have robust relationships with customers. They would have a “sixth sense” if something were “fishy” about a customer, he says.

Boyd insists that the fact that there has been only one allegation of misuse so far is evidence that the company’s vetting and governance model is effective. This, however, ignores the fact that the odds of someone uncovering misuse are low, especially because the company takes care to ensure its spyware won’t be easily detected on infected systems.

All of this, of course, leads to questions about US customers. Based on Paragon’s vetting criteria some might wonder how the current Trump administration would meet it. Given reports of corruption, disregard for the rule of law and Trump’s unveiled threats to use government power against political opponents, fears of misuse by US agencies are not irrational. Asked what the company would do if there were allegations of misuse by a US customer, Boyd said an inspector general or legislative committee would likely investigate the matter, and if they found concrete evidence of misuse, Congress or the company would likely take action.

A year after the acquisition, however, it’s unclear how much US sales have expanded. Shortly before the 2024 acquisition, Paragon signed a $2 million contract with Homeland Security Investigations, a division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, to help dismantle foreign terrorist operations and disrupt fentanyl traffickers, And RedLattice has had longstanding contracts with the US Air Force. But no other government contracts for the companies show up in a search of public databases, though classified contracts likely would not appear. Boyd won’t identify customers but indicates the company is particularly interested in Pentagon and CIA contracts.

“There are offices across the national security enterprise that don't even know they need our product yet,” he says. “And I consider that an unaddressed market.”
